trading-book-vs-banking-book.title: Trading Book vs Banking Book
trading-book-vs-banking-book.summary: The boundary that decides whether a position attracts market-risk or credit-risk capital — and why FRTB made it much harder to cross.

sections.concept:
A bank's balance sheet is split into two regulatory books:

- The **trading book** holds instruments the bank intends to trade, market-make, hedge
  trading positions with, or hold for short-term resale. They are marked to market daily and
  attract **market risk** capital (the MAR standard).
- The **banking book** holds everything else — loans, deposits, held-to-maturity securities,
  most derivatives hedging them. It attracts **credit risk** capital (CRE) and interest-rate
  risk in the banking book is a Pillar 2 matter.

The **boundary** between them is defined in RBC25. It matters because the same bond can
carry very different capital depending on which book it sits in.
sections.why_it_matters:
Before FRTB the boundary was based mainly on the bank's stated *intent*, which made it
porous. During 2007–09 banks held large credit positions in the trading book at low
VaR-based capital, then moved illiquid positions to the banking book when prices fell —
"regulatory arbitrage". FRTB responded by:

- Listing instruments that are *presumed* to be in the trading book and others that *must*
  be in the banking book (RBC25).
- Requiring supervisory approval for reclassification and, where a switch lowers capital,
  imposing a capital surcharge so the bank gains no benefit.
- Making trading-book treatment contingent on daily fair valuation and active management.

For RiskLab, the boundary is the first gate: every SA or IMA calculation applies only to
trading-book positions.
sections.real_world_example:
A bank buys \$100m of an investment-grade corporate bond. Held in the treasury portfolio as a
liquidity asset, it sits in the banking book and is capitalised for credit risk with a
risk weight tied to the issuer's rating. The same bond bought by the credit trading desk to
make markets sits in the trading book: it is marked to market daily and capitalised under
the SA for credit-spread delta (MAR21), default risk (MAR22) and, if applicable, curvature
and vega. The two capital numbers can differ several-fold, which is exactly why the switch
is policed.

mathematical_logic.intro:
The boundary is a classification rule rather than a formula, but it has a quantitative
consequence — total market-risk capital is computed over the trading book only, and a
reclassification that reduces total capital triggers a surcharge equal to the difference:

formulas.caption: Capital is additive across books; the boundary decides which function applies to each position.
A permitted switch that lowers capital earns no benefit — the difference is held as a Pillar 1 surcharge until the position matures or expires.

fx-risk.title: Foreign exchange risk
fx-risk.summary: How currency exposure arises, how it is measured (open position, delta, vega) and where it sits in the FRTB risk classes.

sections.concept:
**FX risk** is the risk that exchange-rate moves change the value of positions denominated in
a currency other than the bank's reporting currency. It arises from:

- **Spot and forward positions** — an *open currency position* (net long or short in each
  currency) that gains or loses one-for-one with the rate;
- **Options** — exposure to the rate (*delta*), to its volatility (*vega*) and to the
  non-linearity of the payoff (*gamma / curvature*);
- **Translation** of foreign-currency assets and liabilities, including the FX component of
  every non-domestic bond, equity or commodity position.

In the FRTB Standardised Approach, FX is one of the seven risk classes (MAR21); in the IMA,
FX rates for specified currency pairs carry a 10-day liquidity horizon and other pairs 20
days (MAR33.12).
sections.why_it_matters:
FX is the risk class every trading book has, because any instrument not in the reporting
currency carries it. Measuring it well matters because:

- FX delta is simple but **FX vega and curvature** on options can dominate the capital of an
  options desk.
- In the SA, FX risk weights and the treatment of **currency pairs** (which pairs count as
  liquid and attract a lower weight) are prescribed in MAR21.
- In the IMA, FX liquidity horizons depend on whether the pair is on the specified list
  (e.g. USD/EUR, USD/JPY, USD/TRY) — a 10- vs 20-day difference is a √2 factor on ES.
sections.real_world_example:
A bank reporting in Turkish lira runs an FX desk long USD 2m, short EUR 1.5m, long GBP 0.5m.
On a day when USD/TRY rises 2% and EUR/TRY rises 1%, the desk makes about 2% × 2m × 30
(spot) on USD and loses 1% × 1.5m × 33 on EUR. Historical simulation applies each of the
last 250 days' moves to today's exposure to build the P&L distribution and read off VaR.
The same desk's option book is priced with Garman–Kohlhagen; bumping spot by one basis
point gives the delta that feeds the SA sensitivities-based method.

value-at-risk.title: Value at Risk (VaR)
value-at-risk.summary: The loss you expect to exceed only rarely — how it is defined, computed and why FRTB demoted it.

sections.concept:
**Value at Risk** answers one question: *over a given horizon, what loss will we exceed only
(1 − α) of the time?* With α = 99% and a one-day horizon, a VaR of \$25,000 means that on
99 days out of 100 the portfolio should lose less than \$25,000 — and on roughly one day in a
hundred it will lose more. VaR says nothing about *how much* more.

VaR is a quantile of the profit-and-loss (P&L) distribution. Everything about a VaR number is
determined by three choices: the **confidence level**, the **horizon**, and **how the P&L
distribution is estimated** (historical, parametric, Monte Carlo).
sections.why_it_matters:
VaR was the regulatory market-risk measure from the 1996 Market Risk Amendment until FRTB.
Banks still run it every day because:

- **Limits.** Trading desks are given VaR limits; breaching one triggers escalation.
- **Backtesting.** FRTB still requires daily VaR at 97.5% and 99% for backtesting (MAR32),
  because a quantile forecast can be checked against realised P&L while ES cannot be checked
  directly.
- **Communication.** A single currency amount at a stated confidence level is easy for
  boards and regulators to understand.

Its weakness — ignoring the size of tail losses and failing sub-additivity — is the reason
FRTB replaced it with Expected Shortfall for *capital* (MAR33.3).
sections.real_world_example:
A market-making desk holds \$1,000,000 of a liquid equity index future. Its daily P&L has a
standard deviation of about 1.2% of the position, i.e. \$12,000. Using the last 500 trading
days as scenarios, the desk ranks the 500 daily P&Ls from worst to best. The 1% worst case
is the 5th-worst day, a loss of about \$25,600. That is the desk's 1-day 99% historical VaR.
If markets have been calm, the number is small; after a volatile quarter it jumps — VaR is
*pro-cyclical*, one reason FRTB insists on stressed calibration.

mathematical_logic.intro:
Let $L = -\text{P\&L}$ be the loss over the horizon. VaR at confidence α is the smallest
loss threshold that is exceeded with probability at most 1 − α:

formulas.caption: Definition as the (1 − α) quantile of P&L, sign-flipped to a positive loss.
Parametric (normal) shortcut with position value V, daily volatility σ, horizon h days.
Historical simulation — the ⌈n(1 − α)⌉-th worst of n scenario P&Ls (interpolation conventions vary).

exercise.title: Historical VaR vs ES on synthetic P&L
exercise.description:
Generate daily P&L scenarios for a \$1,000,000 position and read off VaR and ES. Start with
the normal distribution at 99%, then switch to **Student-t (df = 4)** and watch ES pull away

see how noisy a 99% quantile is on small samples.

expected-shortfall.title: Expected Shortfall (ES)
expected-shortfall.summary: The average loss in the tail beyond VaR — the risk measure FRTB uses for internal-model capital.

sections.concept:
**Expected Shortfall** (also called Conditional VaR or tail loss) is the *average* loss on the
worst (1 − α) of outcomes. Where VaR draws a line and stops, ES walks past the line and asks
how bad it gets on average out there.

At α = 97.5%, ES is the mean of the worst 2.5% of P&L scenarios. If the tail is "thin" (like a
normal distribution) ES is only a little above VaR; if the tail is "fat" (occasional very large
losses) ES can be far above it.
sections.why_it_matters:
FRTB made ES at 97.5% the risk measure for the Internal Models Approach (MAR33.3) for three
reasons:

1. **Tail risk.** The 2008 crisis showed that losses *beyond* VaR were the ones that mattered.
2. **Coherence.** ES is sub-additive, so diversification never increases the measure —
   a property VaR lacks, which made VaR-based limit systems gameable.
3. **Continuity with the past.** 97.5% ES ≈ 99% VaR under normality, so the switch did not by
   itself raise or lower capital for well-behaved portfolios.

ES also underpins the liquidity-horizon formula (MAR33.4), the stressed calibration (MAR33.5)
and the modellable-risk charge IMCC (MAR33.15). Learn it well and the IMA module follows.
sections.real_world_example:
Two desks each report a 99% one-day VaR of \$1m. Desk A trades liquid index futures: on its
worst 1% of days it loses \$1.0–1.3m. Desk B sells deep out-of-the-money options: most days it
earns premium, but on its worst 1% of days it loses \$3–8m. Same VaR, very different risk.
Their 97.5% ES might be \$1.1m and \$4.5m respectively — ES *sees* Desk B's tail. This is
precisely the asymmetry FRTB wanted capital to reflect.

mathematical_logic.intro:
With loss $L = -\text{P\&L}$ and a continuous distribution, ES is the conditional expectation
of the loss given that it exceeds VaR; equivalently it is the average of all VaRs at levels
above α:

formulas.caption: Conditional-expectation definition (continuous case).
Average of the VaRs in the tail — the definition that also works for discrete distributions.
Closed form under the normal distribution; φ is the standard-normal density.
Historical estimator — average of the worst α′n ordered scenarios.

historical-vs-parametric.title: Historical vs parametric models
historical-vs-parametric.summary: Two ways to estimate the same P&L distribution — replaying history or assuming a formula — and what each gets wrong.

sections.concept:
Every VaR or ES number needs a **distribution of P&L**. There are two classic ways to get one:

- **Historical simulation** applies past market moves (e.g. the last 250–500 daily changes in
  rates, spreads, prices) to today's portfolio and reads the quantile or tail mean from the
  resulting scenario P&Ls. No distributional assumption; the data *is* the model.
- **Parametric (variance–covariance)** assumes returns follow a known distribution — almost
  always the normal — estimates volatilities and correlations, and uses closed-form
  expressions ($V\sigma z_\alpha$ for VaR).

Monte Carlo is a third route: simulate many random paths from an assumed model. It shares the
parametric method's reliance on assumptions but can handle non-linear instruments.
sections.why_it_matters:
FRTB does not prescribe a model type (MAR33.9) — but its other requirements push banks toward
historical simulation:

- The stressed calibration (MAR33.5–33.7) is naturally a *window* of history.
- ES at 97.5% is sensitive to tail shape; the normal assumption understates fat tails, so
  parametric ES is rarely accepted for capital.
- Backtesting and P&L attribution (MAR32) compare model P&L to realised P&L, which rewards
  models that reproduce realised market behaviour.

Parametric methods survive for intraday limit monitoring, quick what-if analysis and as a
sanity check on the full model.
sections.real_world_example:
In early 2020 a parametric model calibrated on the previous year's calm data produced a 99%
equity VaR near 1.5% of position value. In March 2020 daily index moves of 8–12% occurred on
several days — eight-to-ten-standard-deviation events under the normal assumption, which
should "never" happen. A historical-simulation model with a 500-day window picked the moves up
within days as they entered the window; a stressed window including 2008 already had them.
Age-weighted historical VaR (Boudoukh–Richardson–Whitelaw) reacts faster still by giving
recent scenarios more weight — at the cost of being *more* pro-cyclical.

mathematical_logic.intro: Both methods estimate the same quantile; the difference is where the distribution comes from.

why-frtb.title: Why Basel introduced FRTB
why-frtb.summary: The failures of the Basel 2.5 market-risk framework in 2007–09 and the design choices the Fundamental Review made in response.

sections.why_it_matters:
The crisis exposed four problems with VaR-based capital:

1. **Tail risk was invisible.** 99% VaR ignored how large losses beyond the quantile were.
2. **Illiquidity was ignored.** A 10-day horizon for everything let banks hold illiquid
   credit positions at low capital.
3. **The boundary was gameable.** Positions migrated to whichever book carried less capital.
4. **Standardised and internal models were not comparable.** Banks' internal-model capital
   varied widely for similar portfolios, and the old standardised approach was too crude to
   act as a credible floor.

Basel 2.5 (2009) patched this with stressed VaR, the Incremental Risk Charge and the
Comprehensive Risk Measure, roughly tripling market-risk capital — but it was a patch. FRTB
rebuilt the framework.
sections.real_world_example:
In 2007–08 several large banks reported trading losses many times their VaR, on positions
(super-senior CDO tranches, leveraged loans) that could not be sold for months. Under
Basel 2.5 those positions attracted VaR + stressed VaR + IRC. Under FRTB the same book would
face ES at 97.5% calibrated to the stress period, 60–120-day liquidity horizons for
credit-spread risk, an SA-based floor via the fallback, and a desk-level approval that
could be withdrawn if backtesting or P&L attribution failed.

mathematical_logic.intro: FRTB's key quantitative substitutions can be summarised side by side.

formulas.caption: Pre-FRTB internal-model capital — VaR plus stressed VaR with multipliers, plus incremental and comprehensive risk charges.
Modellable-risk capital — stressed, liquidity-adjusted ES, half diversified / half undiversified (MAR33.15), plus SES for non-modellable factors and the DRC.
Why the confidence level moved from 99% to 97.5% without a mechanical capital change.

exercise.description:
Run the simulator with the **normal** distribution at 99% and note VaR. Switch to
**Student-t (df = 4)** keeping the same volatility: VaR rises a little, ES rises much more.
This gap — risk beyond the quantile — is what Basel 2.5 capital could not see.

questions.stem: Which was NOT a weakness of the pre-FRTB framework identified by the Basel Committee?
choices: VaR ignored losses beyond the quantile
The trading book boundary was easy to arbitrage
Capital requirements were too high for all banks
questions.rationale: The Committee's concern was under-capitalisation and incomparability, not excessive capital.

questions.stem: Under FRTB, internal-model approval is granted…
questions.rationale: MAR12 defines the desk and MAR32 tests apply desk by desk.

questions.stem: Why must every FRTB bank compute the Standardised Approach even if it uses internal models?
choices: For disclosure comparability and as the fallback when desks fail IMA tests
Because the SA is always lower
questions.rationale: The SA is the fallback and the basis for comparability across banks.

questions.stem: Basel 2.5 (2009) added…
choices: the Incremental Risk Charge and the Comprehensive Risk Measure
questions.rationale: Basel 2.5 was the interim patch; ES, liquidity horizons, SBM and desk approval came with FRTB.

liquidity-horizons.title: Liquidity horizons
liquidity-horizons.summary: Why FRTB measures different risk factors over 10, 20, 40, 60 or 120 days, and how the MAR33.4 formula stretches a 10-day ES.

sections.concept:
A **liquidity horizon** is the time a bank would need to exit or hedge a risk position in a
stressed market without moving the price against itself. Basel 2.5 assumed 10 days for
everything. FRTB recognises that a USD interest-rate swap can be hedged in days while a
high-yield credit spread, an exotic commodity volatility or a small-cap equity position may
take months.

Every risk factor is mapped to one of five horizons — **10, 20, 40, 60 or 120 days** — by
risk class and liquidity tier (MAR33.12, Table 2). The Expected Shortfall is then computed
so that each risk factor is shocked over *its* horizon.
sections.why_it_matters:
Liquidity horizons are one of the largest drivers of IMA capital:

- A 60-day horizon multiplies a 10-day ES by up to √6 ≈ 2.45; a 120-day horizon by up to √12 ≈ 3.46.
- They penalise illiquid risk even inside an approved model, which Basel 2.5 did not.
- They interact with the modellability test (MAR31): a non-modellable factor leaves the ES
  model and is capitalised through SES with a *minimum* 20-day horizon (MAR33.16).
- Operationally, the nested ES calculation (MAR33.4) multiplies the number of ES runs a bank
  must perform every night.
sections.real_world_example:
A rates desk holds USD swaps (10-day), a position in Polish zloty swaps (unspecified currency
→ 20-day) and some swaption vega (interest-rate volatility → 60-day). Its 10-day ES with all
factors shocked is \$1.0m. Shocking only PLN rates and the vega gives \$0.5m; shocking only the
vega gives \$0.3m. The MAR33.4 formula turns these three numbers into a single
liquidity-adjusted ES of about \$1.27m — more than \$1.0m because of the slow-to-hedge factors,
but far less than \$2.45m because only part of the risk sits at 60 days.

mathematical_logic.intro:
MAR33.4 starts from a base horizon T = 10 days and adds horizon increments in quadrature.
$ES_T(P)$ shocks all factors; $ES_T(P,j)$ shocks only factors with horizon ≥ $LH_j$.

formulas.caption: MAR33.4 liquidity-adjusted ES, with LH = (10, 20, 40, 60, 120) and T = 10.

formulas.latex: \mathrm{ES} = ES_T(P)\,\sqrt{LH_k / T}\quad\text{if every factor has horizon } LH_k
formulas.caption: Single-horizon special case — plain square-root-of-time scaling.
The five scaling factors for the increments 10, 10, 20, 20 and 60 days.

exercise.title: Stretch a 10-day ES across the five horizons
exercise.description:
Enter the nested ES values (they must be non-increasing as the horizon grows if the excluded
factors add risk). Watch the uplift: setting every bucket equal to the base ES reproduces
√12 ≈ 3.46× — the whole book at 120 days. Setting all buckets to zero leaves the base ES
unchanged — everything hedgeable in ten days. Most real desks sit between 1.1× and 1.8×.

MAR33.2.title: ES must be computed daily, bank-wide and per IMA desk
MAR33.2.excerpt: Expected Shortfall must be computed on a daily basis, both for the bank-wide internal model and for each trading desk that uses the internal models approach.
MAR33.2.plain_language: A bank using its own model cannot run it once a month. Every business day it must produce an ES number for the whole bank *and* a separate one for each desk that has model approval. The daily cadence feeds the backtesting and P&L attribution tests in MAR32 and the 60-day averaging in the capital formula.
MAR33.2.technical_interpretation: Daily computation at desk level is what makes desk-level approval (MAR12, MAR32) operational: the desk's own ES, backtesting exceptions and PLA metrics are all produced from the same daily run. Operationally this requires end-of-day positions, a risk-factor time series updated at least quarterly (MAR33.8) and a full-revaluation or sensitivity-based P&L engine that can run inside the overnight batch.
MAR33.2.mathematical_implications: The daily series $ES_t$ is the input to the time-averaging in the capital calculation, so a single bad day is smoothed but not ignored. It is also why the ES must be a *reproducible* function of positions and scenarios: two runs on the same inputs must agree.

MAR33.3.title: 97.5th percentile, one-tailed confidence level for ES
MAR33.3.excerpt: In calculating ES, a bank must use a 97.5th percentile, one-tailed confidence level.
MAR33.3.plain_language: Under Basel 2.5 the risk measure was VaR at 99%. FRTB replaced it with Expected Shortfall at 97.5%: instead of asking "what is the loss we exceed only 1% of the time", we ask "what is the *average* loss on the worst 2.5% of days". For a normal distribution the two numbers are almost identical, which is exactly why 97.5% was chosen — the switch does not mechanically inflate capital, it changes *what* is measured.
MAR33.3.technical_interpretation: ES is coherent (sub-additive), so diversified portfolios never attract more capital than the sum of their parts, and it is sensitive to the shape of the tail beyond the quantile. The 97.5% level is applied to the 10-day base horizon ES and to every liquidity-horizon component in MAR33.4, and to the stressed calibration in MAR33.5. Backtesting (MAR32) still uses VaR at both 97.5% and 99% because ES itself is hard to backtest.
MAR33.3.mathematical_implications: For a loss distribution $L$: $ES_{0.975} = \mathbb{E}[L \mid L \ge VaR_{0.975}]$. Under normality $ES_{0.975} = \sigma\,\varphi(z_{0.975})/0.025 \approx 2.338\,\sigma$ while $VaR_{0.99} = 2.326\,\sigma$: a difference of about 0.5%. Under fat tails (Student-t with 4 degrees of freedom) the ratio $ES_{0.975}/VaR_{0.99}$ rises well above 1 — the **Historical VaR & ES simulator** lets you see this directly.

MAR33.4.title: Liquidity-horizon scaling of ES from a 10-day base horizon
MAR33.4.excerpt: Liquidity horizons must be reflected by scaling an ES calculated on a base horizon of 10 days. The ES for a position set P is computed as the square root of the sum of the squared base ES and, for each liquidity-horizon bucket j ≥ 2, the squared ES of the risk factors with liquidity horizon at least LH_j, scaled by the square root of (LH_j − LH_{j−1}) / 10. Table 1 lists the horizons 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days.
MAR33.4.plain_language: Not every risk can be hedged or sold in ten days. A large-cap equity position can; a high-yield credit spread or an exotic commodity volatility cannot. FRTB therefore assigns each risk factor a *liquidity horizon* and stretches the 10-day ES so that slow-moving risks are measured over a longer holding period. Instead of re-running the model at 20, 40, 60 and 120 days, the formula builds the longer-horizon ES from a sequence of 10-day ES calculations on shrinking subsets of risk factors.
MAR33.4.technical_interpretation: $ES_T(P)$ is the 10-day ES with all risk factors shocked. $ES_T(P,j)$ is the 10-day ES when only risk factors with liquidity horizon ≥ $LH_j$ are shocked and the others are frozen. Each increment $(LH_j - LH_{j-1})$ is scaled by square-root-of-time and the increments are combined in quadrature, which implicitly assumes the P&L over successive 10-day windows is uncorrelated. In practice banks compute $ES_T(P,j)$ by nesting the risk-factor subsets, so five ES runs (full set, LH ≥ 20, ≥ 40, ≥ 60, ≥ 120) are needed per calculation, each for current and stressed calibration and for the full and reduced risk-factor sets.
MAR33.4.mathematical_implications: $$ES = \sqrt{ES_T(P)^2 + \sum_{j \ge 2}\left(ES_T(P,j)\sqrt{\tfrac{LH_j - LH_{j-1}}{T}}\right)^2}, \qquad T = 10$$ If every risk factor has the same horizon $LH_k$, the nested ES values coincide and the expression collapses to $ES_T(P)\sqrt{LH_k/10}$: a 60-day book carries $\sqrt 6 \approx 2.45\times$ its 10-day ES. Because the terms add in quadrature, moving a small portion of risk to a long horizon costs much less than moving all of it — try it in the **Liquidity-horizon ES scaling** calculator.

MAR33.5.title: ES calibrated to a period of stress using a reduced set of risk factors
MAR33.5.excerpt: The ES measure must be calibrated to a period of significant financial stress. Because full risk-factor histories rarely reach back to the stress period, the calibration is done with a reduced set of risk factors that must explain at least 75% of the variation of the full ES model, subject to supervisory approval.
MAR33.5.plain_language: A model calibrated to calm recent markets understates risk. Basel 2.5 fixed this by adding a separate "stressed VaR" on top of normal VaR. FRTB goes further: the *only* ES that matters for capital is the stressed one. Since many risk factors (new issuers, new indices) have no data from 2008, the bank is allowed to use a smaller set of long-history factors as long as that set captures at least three-quarters of the full model's risk.
MAR33.5.technical_interpretation: Define $ES_{F,C}$ (full set, current period), $ES_{R,C}$ (reduced set, current period) and $ES_{R,S}$ (reduced set, stress period). MAR33.6 then scales the reduced-set stressed ES back up to the full set: $ES = ES_{R,S} \cdot ES_{F,C}/ES_{R,C}$ with the ratio floored at 1. The 75% test is a model-adequacy test of the reduced set, assessed over a defined window.
MAR33.5.mathematical_implications: $$ES = ES_{R,S}\times\max\!\left(1,\ \frac{ES_{F,C}}{ES_{R,C}}\right)$$ The ratio is a proxy for the risk the reduced set misses; flooring it at 1 means a reduced set that happens to be riskier than the full set gives no capital relief.

MAR33.7.title: Identifying the 12-month stress period
MAR33.7.excerpt: Banks must identify the 12-month period of stress over the observation horizon in which the portfolio experiences the largest loss, searching back at least to 2007, with observations equally weighted, and must update the identification at least quarterly.
MAR33.7.plain_language: The stress period is not a fixed date chosen by regulators; it is whichever continuous year since 2007 would have hurt *this* portfolio the most. A rates-heavy book may find its worst year in 2022, an equity book in 2008–09, a credit book in 2020. Because the portfolio changes, the search has to be repeated at least every quarter.
MAR33.7.technical_interpretation: The search is a rolling-window optimisation over the reduced risk-factor set (MAR33.5): for each candidate 12-month window compute the ES of the current portfolio and pick the maximum. Equal weighting rules out exponential decay schemes (contrast age-weighted VaR, which RiskLab includes as an educational calculator) inside the stress window.
MAR33.7.mathematical_implications: $$\text{stress window} = \arg\max_{w \in \mathcal W} ES_{R}\big(P_{\text{today}},\, w\big)$$ where $\mathcal W$ is the set of 12-month windows from 2007 to today. The result is a portfolio-specific quantity, so two banks with different books will legitimately use different stress periods.

MAR33.9.title: No prescribed model type (historical simulation, Monte Carlo or analytical)
MAR33.9.excerpt: No particular type of ES model is prescribed. Historical simulation, Monte Carlo simulation or other analytical methods are acceptable provided the model captures all material risks and meets the backtesting and P&L attribution requirements.
MAR33.9.plain_language: Regulators care about outcomes, not technique. A bank can replay history, simulate thousands of random futures, or use closed-form approximations — as long as the resulting ES captures the risks it runs and the model passes the MAR32 tests.
MAR33.9.technical_interpretation: In practice most IMA banks use (filtered) historical simulation because it needs no distributional assumption and makes the stress-period calibration (MAR33.5–33.7) natural. Monte Carlo is common for path-dependent options. Parametric methods are rare for ES because tail shape matters more than for VaR.
MAR33.9.mathematical_implications: Whatever the method, the output is a loss distribution from which $ES_{0.975}$ is read. The **Historical VaR & ES simulator** and the **Parametric VaR & ES** calculators show the same statistic computed two ways and why they diverge under fat tails.

MAR33.12.title: Mapping risk factors to liquidity horizon categories (Table 2)
MAR33.12.excerpt: Each risk factor must be mapped to one of the risk factor categories in Table 2 using a consistent, documented and validated procedure. The liquidity horizon is a floor (a bank may, with approval, use a longer one) and is capped at the maturity of the instrument.
MAR33.12.plain_language: This is the lookup table behind MAR33.4. Interest rates in major currencies and large-cap equities get 10 days; high-yield corporate credit spreads get 60; credit-spread volatility and exotic commodity volatility get 120. A bank cannot shorten a horizon, but a position maturing in 30 days need not be measured over 60.
MAR33.12.technical_interpretation: The mapping is part of the risk-factor taxonomy and must be validated like any model input. Categories mix *asset class* (rates, credit, equity, FX, commodity), *liquidity tier* (specified vs other currencies, IG vs HY, large vs small cap) and *risk type* (price vs volatility vs "other"). Volatility and "other" types always carry a longer horizon than the underlying price.
MAR33.12.mathematical_implications: The table determines the nesting in MAR33.4: factors with horizon $n$ appear in every $ES_T(P,j)$ with $LH_j \le n$. A risk factor at 120 days contributes to all five terms, one at 10 days only to the first. The full table is stored in RiskLab's engine as `params/mar33_liquidity_horizons.json` and rendered on the **Liquidity horizons** topic page.

MAR33.13.title: Unconstrained bank-wide ES across all modellable risk factors (IMCC(C))
MAR33.13.excerpt: The bank-wide internal ES model must include all modellable risk factors and may be computed without supervisory constraints on cross-risk-class correlations; the resulting stressed ES is the unconstrained term IMCC(C).
MAR33.13.plain_language: The first half of the modellable capital charge lets the bank's model use its own view of diversification across rates, credit, equity, FX and commodities.
MAR33.13.technical_interpretation: IMCC(C) is the stressed, liquidity-adjusted ES (MAR33.4–33.7) of the whole modellable book. It is the "diversified" number; MAR33.14 produces the "undiversified" partner.
MAR33.13.mathematical_implications: $IMCC(C) = ES_{R,S}(P)\cdot\max\!\big(1, ES_{F,C}(P)/ES_{R,C}(P)\big)$ with full cross-class diversification.

MAR33.14.title: Partial ES per broad risk class with other risk factors held constant
MAR33.14.excerpt: A partial ES is calculated for each broad regulatory risk class (interest rate, equity, FX, commodity, credit spread) by shocking only that class's risk factors and holding all others constant; the partial ES values are summed to give the constrained aggregate.
MAR33.14.plain_language: The second half of the charge assumes *no* diversification between asset classes: compute the ES of the rates book alone, the equity book alone, and so on, then add them up.
MAR33.14.technical_interpretation: Each partial ES follows the same stressed, liquidity-adjusted recipe. Summing across classes is equivalent to assuming correlation +1 between class-level losses, the most conservative aggregation.
MAR33.14.mathematical_implications: $\sum_i IMCC(C_i)$ where $i$ runs over the five broad risk classes. By sub-additivity of ES, $\sum_i IMCC(C_i) \ge IMCC(C)$.

MAR33.15.title: IMCC — weighted average of constrained and unconstrained ES (ρ = 0.5)
MAR33.15.excerpt: The aggregate capital requirement for modellable risk factors (IMCC) is a weighted average of the unconstrained ES and the sum of the partial ES values by risk class, with the weight ρ set at 0.5.
MAR33.15.plain_language: Regulators split the difference: half the credit for the bank's own diversification view, half for the no-diversification view. A bank whose model claims very large diversification benefits only gets to keep half of them.
MAR33.15.technical_interpretation: This is the FRTB replacement for the Basel 2.5 practice of simply summing VaR and stressed VaR. Because the constrained sum is always at least the unconstrained ES, IMCC lies between $IMCC(C)$ and $\sum_i IMCC(C_i)$ and is at least the unconstrained ES.
MAR33.15.mathematical_implications: $$IMCC = \rho \cdot IMCC(C) + (1-\rho)\sum_{i=1}^{5} IMCC(C_i), \qquad \rho = 0.5$$ The **SA vs IMA comparison engine** (Phase 5) exposes ρ as an educational slider so the effect of the supervisory correlation constraint on capital can be seen directly.

MAR33.15.chapter_title: Internal models approach: capital requirements calculation

MAR33.16.title: Non-modellable risk factors capitalised with stress scenarios (SES)
MAR33.16.excerpt: Each non-modellable risk factor must be capitalised using a stress scenario calibrated to be at least as prudent as the ES calibration, with a common 12-month stress period per broad risk class and a liquidity horizon of at least 20 days; where no acceptable stress scenario can be found, the maximum possible loss is used.
MAR33.16.plain_language: A risk factor that fails the eligibility test in MAR31 (too few real price observations) cannot go into the ES model. Instead the bank must work out how much it could lose on that factor in a stressed year and hold that amount — with far less diversification benefit than modellable risks enjoy (see MAR33.17).
MAR33.16.technical_interpretation: The stress scenario risk measure SES is computed per NMRF over its liquidity horizon (floor 20 days), calibrated to the same type of stress window used for ES but chosen per risk class. Idiosyncratic equity and credit-spread NMRFs may be aggregated with zero correlation; all other NMRFs are aggregated with a correlation parameter ρ = 0.6 (MAR33.17).
MAR33.16.mathematical_implications: Each $SES_k$ is a loss at a 97.5%-equivalent stress; the aggregate is roughly $\sqrt{\rho(\sum_k SES_k)^2 + (1-\rho)\sum_k SES_k^2}$ for the non-idiosyncratic set (exact formula in MAR33.17, Phase 4). Because this sits *outside* the IMCC diversification, an NMRF-heavy desk can see capital rise sharply when a factor loses modellability — a scenario the Phase 5 comparison engine simulates.

MAR33.17.title: Aggregation of stress scenario capital (SES) across NMRFs
MAR33.17.excerpt: The aggregate SES combines idiosyncratic credit-spread and equity NMRFs aggregated with zero correlation and all other NMRFs aggregated with a correlation parameter ρ of 0.6.
MAR33.17.plain_language: Zero correlation for pure name-specific risks, 0.6 for everything else — a middle ground between "add them all up" (ρ = 1) and "they fully diversify" (ρ = 0).
MAR33.17.technical_interpretation: The exact aggregation expression is set out in the paragraph as a formula; RiskLab will transcribe and implement it in Phase 4 (IMA Lab — NMRF/SES simulator) with a validation record. Until then this page records the structural facts only.

MAR33.17.chapter_title: Internal models approach: capital requirements calculation

MAR33.22.title: IMA default risk charge — greater of 12-week average and latest measure
MAR33.22.excerpt: The default risk capital requirement under the IMA is the greater of the average of the DRC model measures over the previous 12 weeks and the most recent DRC model measure.
MAR33.22.plain_language: Default risk in the trading book (the chance an issuer actually defaults, not just that its spread widens) is modelled separately from ES, at a 99.9% level over one year, and its capital charge is smoothed over roughly a quarter — but can never fall below the latest number.
MAR33.22.technical_interpretation: The DRC model (MAR33.18–33.27) is a weekly default-simulation VaR with two systematic factors, PD floors of 0.03% and correlations calibrated to 10 years including a stress period. The "greater of" rule parallels the 60-day averaging used for ES-based capital and prevents a one-off low reading from reducing capital.
